docs.title: MBA rough notes
docs.text:
MBA from AI rough notes

THE CISO-MBA: COURSE CATALOG

BLOCK I — THE MBA CORE (the standard first-year canon, each taught through a security-executive lens)

  1. Financial Accounting MBA content: reading income statements, balance sheets, cash flow statements CISO customization: security as a line item — how breaches hit financials (material incident disclosures per SEC rules), how auditors treat IT controls, SOX 404 Free resources: Khan Academy financial accounting; MIT OCW 15.501 Deliverable: pick a public company, read their 10-K, find every security-related disclosure and write a 2-page memo on how security affected their financials

  2. Corporate Finance and Budgeting MBA content: NPV, ROI, CAPM, capital budgeting, cost of capital CISO customization: building and defending a security budget, cost-benefit analysis for controls, security insurance, ransomware payment decisions, SANS SEC405 (Business Finance Essentials) covers exactly this Free resources: Khan Academy finance and capital markets; Aswath Damodaran's free NYU valuation lectures (online, all public) Deliverable: a full annual security budget for a 2,000-person company, with an ROI justification for each major line

  3. Marketing MBA content: segmentation, positioning, the 4 Ps, buyer psychology CISO customization: this is the CISO's secret weapon course — you "market" to three audiences: the board (buy-in for budget), employees (security awareness behavior change), and customers (trust as a selling point). Awareness campaigns ARE marketing campaigns. Free resources: Coursera Wharton "Introduction to Marketing" (audit free); "Influence" by Cialdini Deliverable: a security awareness campaign designed like a real marketing campaign — target segments, message, channels, and metrics for behavior change

  4. Microeconomics and Strategy MBA content: supply and demand, game theory, Porter's Five Forces, competitive advantage CISO customization: threat modeling as economics — attackers are rational actors who respond to incentives; security as competitive advantage (why AWS and banks sell trust); game theory applied to attacker/defender dynamics Free resources: Khan Academy economics; MIT OCW 15.010 or Yale's open microeconomics course; Porter's "Competitive Strategy" Deliverable: a threat actor economic analysis — what does an attack cost the attacker, what's their ROI, which controls change their calculus

  5. Operations Management MBA content: process design, queues, capacity planning, quality management, supply chain CISO customization: the security program IS an operation — SOC staffing models, incident response as a process, vulnerability management pipelines, SLAs. Supply chain becomes third-party/vendor risk (SolarWinds is a supply chain operations failure, not a tooling failure). Free resources: MIT OCW 15.761; Coursera Wharton operations (audit free) Deliverable: a process map of a vuln management program from scan to fix, with cycle time metrics and bottlenecks

  6. Organizational Behavior and Leadership MBA content: motivation, team dynamics, power and influence, managing up CISO customization: influencing without authority (the CISO usually owns risk but controls almost nothing), building the security team, handling the org's immune response to change, incident command psychology Free resources: Coursera "Organizational Analysis" (Stanford, audit free); "The Effective Executive" (Drucker); "Extreme Ownership" Deliverable: an org design for a security function — roles, reporting lines, where CISO reports and why it matters

  7. Business Law, Ethics, and Negotiation MBA content: contracts, liability, regulatory regimes, bargaining CISO customization: breach notification law, GDPR/CCPA, sector regs (HIPAA/SOX/PCI — pick your target industry), vendor contract security clauses, negotiating with auditors, regulators, and (during incidents) cyber insurers and law enforcement Free resources: any state university's open business law text; Harvard's Program on Negotiation free articles Deliverable: a playbook for the legal first 48 hours of a breach

  8. Data and Statistics (MBA "quant") MBA content: regression, distributions, decision analysis, dashboards CISO customization: metrics that matter — risk quantification (FAIR — this is your anchor text), measuring control effectiveness, board-level KPIs vs operational metrics, why risk heat maps lie Free resources: Khan Academy statistics; FAIR book (Jones, "Measuring and ManagingInformation Risk") Deliverable: a quantified risk register with dollar-value exposures instead of red/yellow/green

BLOCK II — CISO ELECTIVES (second-year specialization)

  1. IT and Vendor Management: contracting, SLAs, TCO analysis — Deliverable: a real RFP evaluation for a SIEM
  2. Corporate Governance: board structure, audit committees, director duties — Deliverable: a board presentation deck on a major security investment
  3. Crisis Management and Communications: PR side of breaches — Deliverable: holding statements for a breach scenario, drafted before it happens
  4. Entrepreneurship (optional but valuable): how startups and VCs evaluate security — useful if you ever want a CISO-in-residence or advisory path

CAPSTONE

Write a complete security program for a real or fictional mid-size company: strategy doc, budget, org chart, quantified risk register, board deck, and a 91-day onboarding plan. Andy Ellis's free "How to CISO" volumes (howtociso.com) are the best template for this. This becomes your portfolio.

docs.title: Law
docs.text:
Law deserves more than the one-block slot I gave it — I'd promote it to a full standalone course, and current events prove why: the two landmark CISO personal-liability cases resolved recently in opposite directions. The SEC's case against SolarWinds and its CISO Tim Brown (targeting him over cyber disclosures) was dismissed with prejudice in November 2025. But Uber CSO Joe Sullivan's conviction for obstruction and misprision over the 2016 breach handling held up. Lesson: securities-law theories against CISOs are getting beaten back, but personal criminal exposure for covering up or mishandling a breach is real. A modern CISO course treats law as self-defense.

Here's the expanded law course for your CISO-MBA.

CISO-MBA COURSE 7 (EXPANDED): LAW FOR SECURITY EXECUTIVES

Module A: The law you operate under - Breach notification: state laws (all 50 US states have them), GDPR's 72-hour rule, SEC's cyber disclosure rules for public companies (4-item 8-K) - Privacy regimes: GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, and whichever regs apply to your target industry — HIPAA (health), GLBA (finance), PCI DSS (contractual, not law, but enforced like it) - Regulatory agencies and what they can do to you: SEC, FTC, state AGs, HHS OCR, EU DPAs - Study method: don't read statutes — read enforcement actions. FTC consent decrees and SEC litigation releases are short, factual, and show exactly what conduct gets punished

Module B: The law of personal exposure (the new stuff) - The two cases every CISO must know cold: Uber (Sullivan — convicted and it stuck; the crime wasn't the breach, it was the concealment) and SolarWinds (Brown — SEC case dismissed, but only after two years and presumably seven figures of personal legal costs) - Practical output: what to demand in your employment contract — indemnification, D&O insurance that explicitly covers you, right to counsel. This is now a standard CISO negotiation item - Privilege basics: how to work with outside counsel during an incident so your forensics are privileged

Module C: Contracts and commercial law - Security clauses in vendor contracts: breach notification terms, liability caps, right to audit - Your own paper: when you buy security products, who bears the loss when they fail - Cyber insurance: what policies actually cover, and how your incident response affects whether they pay out

Module D: Incident law — the 48 hours - When a breach happens, lawyers run the response and you work for them. Know the sequence: outside counsel engaged, privilege established, then investigation - Who you must notify and when; the crimes of timing — notifying too late is itself the violation - Regulatory relations: first contact with a regulator, negotiating exam scope, consent orders

Module E: Governance and fiduciary duty - What a board legally owes shareholders regarding cyber risk, and what you owe the board - Duty of care vs business judgment rule: boards are allowed to accept risk; your job is to make sure they do it knowingly - Documentation: a defensible paper trail of your risk advice. "I advised in writing, they accepted in writing" is the shield

Resources, all free - Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance (corpgov.law.harvard.edu) — superb CISO-relevant analysis, including their December 2025 piece on the SolarWinds dismissal - SEC.gov litigation releases and enforcement actions - IAPP (privacy professionals' org) — free articles and US privacy law maps - FTC enforcement actions (ftc.gov/legal-library) - Krebs on Security and Digital Lawyering newsletters for following cases as they happen

Deliverable (this one matters most) Build your own incident legal playbook: notification decision tree (which breach triggers which law in which jurisdiction and at what deadline), a privilege protocol, a personal-indemnity checklist for your next employment contract, and a one-page memo you'd give a new CEO on day one explaining the legal exposure structure of the company.
